title: Adaptations: how living things are suited to heat, cold, water and darkness

summary.text: A camel can go for days in the Thar Desert without a drink. A snow leopard sleeps on ice in Ladakh. A fish breathes under water, and a cave fish finds food in total darkness. Each of them has features that solve the problems of its own place. A feature like this is called an adaptation. Desert plants keep their water with fat stems and waxy skins, because water escapes only through a surface that touches the air. Cold-place animals keep their warmth with thick fur, fat, small ears and huddling. Water animals have fins, webbed feet and oily feathers. Night and cave animals have huge eyes, shining eyes, whiskers, or senses that work with no light at all. Adaptations are passed down from parents to young, and build up over many, many generations.
summary.art: A picture split into four: a camel resting in Thar sand under a hot sun, a snow leopard on a snowy Ladakh rock with its long tail wrapped round it, a duck paddling with webbed feet, and a pale cave fish in a dark cave pool.

intro.hook: Look at the washing on your line. A shirt pegged out flat dries by lunch. A towel left bundled up in a bucket is still damp at night. Both got just as wet. So why does one dry so much more slowly? What do you think?
intro.text: A cactus in a hot desert has the same problem as the washing. Water slowly escapes from it into the dry air. A cactus that loses water too fast dries up and dies. In this unit you find out how a cactus keeps its water, how a camel lives with little water, and how a snow leopard stays warm in the snow. You also find out how fish and ducks are suited to water, and how some animals find their food in total darkness.
intro.art: A balcony washing line with a shirt pegged out flat in the sun, and below it a bucket with a damp towel bundled up inside.

outcomes: I can say what an adaptation is, and tell it apart from a body getting used to a place, which is called acclimatising.
I can explain how plants and animals of hot, dry places keep cool and save water, with the camel, the cactus and the desert fox as examples.
I can explain how animals of cold places keep warm: fur, fat, small ears and huddling, with the snow leopard, the yak and the penguin as examples.
I can explain how living things are suited to water: fins, webbed feet, oily feathers, breathing roots and air-filled stems.
I can explain how animals find their way and their food in the dark: big eyes, eyeshine, whiskers, the fish's lateral line and echolocation.
I can run a fair test with three wet paper towels, and explain why their shape and a covering change how fast water escapes.
I can tell the true story of how Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen showed that a camel's hump is fat, not a water tank.

terms.meaning: The place where a living thing lives, which gives it food, water, shelter and the right warmth.
terms.example: The Thar Desert is the habitat of the camel. A pond is the habitat of a frog.
terms.art: A camel in sand dunes next to a frog in a green pond.

terms.meaning: A feature of a living thing's body, or a way it behaves, that helps it live and have young in its habitat. Adaptations are passed from parents to their young.
terms.example: A camel's wide, padded feet do not sink in soft sand. That is an adaptation to the desert.
terms.art: A close-up of a camel's wide, soft foot pressing on sand without sinking.

terms.meaning: To get used to a new place within your own life. Your body changes a little, but these changes are not passed on to your children.
terms.example: A family from Kochi who moves to Delhi starts to sweat sooner and drink more after a week or two of hot summer days.
terms.art: A child on a hot day drinking from a steel tumbler, with a calendar showing two weeks crossed off.

terms.meaning: When water evaporates, it turns into an invisible gas, water vapour, and goes into the air.
terms.example: Wet clothes on a line dry because their water evaporates.
terms.art: Clothes on a balcony line with faint wavy lines rising from them.

terms.meaning: The outside of a thing, where it touches the air or water around it.
terms.example: A sheet of paper spread flat has a big surface. Rolled up tight, most of its surface is hidden inside.
terms.art: A flat sheet of paper next to the same sheet rolled into a tube.

terms.meaning: A plant with thick, juicy leaves or stems that store water. Cactuses and aloe vera are succulents.
terms.example: Break an aloe vera leaf, and a clear, slimy jelly full of water oozes out.
terms.art: A potted aloe vera plant with one thick leaf broken, showing clear jelly.

terms.meaning: A thin, waterproof layer on the outside of leaves and stems. Scientists call it the cuticle. It slows down the water escaping from a plant.
terms.example: Water drops roll into beads on a cabbage leaf, because the leaf has a waxy coat.
terms.art: Water drops sitting as round beads on a pale green cabbage leaf.

terms.meaning: Tiny holes in a leaf, too small to see without a microscope. Air goes in and out through them, and water vapour escapes through them. A plant can open and close them.
terms.example: A cactus opens its stomata at night, when the air is cooler and less water escapes.
terms.art: A magnified leaf surface with tiny mouth-shaped holes, some open and some closed.

terms.meaning: A layer that slows down heat moving from a warm place to a cold place.
terms.example: A snow leopard's thick fur is insulation. It slows down the heat escaping from its warm body into the icy air.
terms.art: A snow leopard lying on a snowy rock, with a cut-away showing its thick fur.

terms.meaning: A thick layer of fat under the skin of whales, seals and some other animals. It works as insulation in icy water.
terms.example: Seals rest on ice and swim in freezing seas, kept warm by the blubber under their skin.
terms.art: A cut-away drawing of a whale's side, showing skin, a thick yellow fat layer and muscle.

terms.meaning: When animals crowd close together, so that less of each body faces the cold air.
terms.example: Emperor penguins huddle in a big crowd through the Antarctic winter.
terms.art: Hundreds of emperor penguins crowded tightly together in a snowstorm.

terms.meaning: Awake and active at night, and resting by day.
terms.example: Owls, bats and the slender loris are nocturnal.
terms.art: A slender loris with huge round eyes holding a branch under the Moon.

terms.meaning: The glow of an animal's eyes when a light shines on them in the dark. It comes from a shiny layer at the back of the eye that reflects light back through it.
terms.example: A cat's eyes shine green in a torch beam at night. Human eyes do not shine like that.
terms.art: Two glowing green eyes in a dark garden, caught in a torch beam.

terms.meaning: Long, stiff hairs on the face of animals like cats, rats and seals. They feel the air and things nearby, even in the dark.
terms.example: A cat pokes its head into a gap, and its whiskers touch the sides first.
terms.art: A cat's face close-up, with its long whiskers spread out.

terms.meaning: A row of tiny sensors along each side of a fish's body. It feels the water moving, so a fish can sense other animals nearby without seeing them.
terms.example: A blind cave fish swims round a rock without bumping it, using its lateral line.
terms.art: A fish with a dotted line drawn along its side, from gills to tail.

terms.meaning: Finding things by making sounds and listening to the echoes that bounce back.
terms.example: Bats and dolphins use echolocation to find food in the dark or in muddy water.
terms.art: A bat flying at night, with curved sound waves going out and echoes coming back from a moth.

terms.meaning: Shaped so that water or air slides past easily: smooth, rounded at the front and narrow at the back.
terms.example: A fish's body is streamlined, so it can swim fast with little effort.
terms.art: A side view of a fish with smooth lines of water flowing past it.

terms.meaning: Feet with skin stretched between the toes, which push against water like a paddle.
terms.example: Ducks, frogs and otters have webbed feet.
terms.art: A duck's orange webbed foot spread out under water.

terms.meaning: A small gland near the base of a bird's tail that makes oil. The bird spreads the oil over its feathers with its beak.
terms.example: Ducks preen often, so water runs off their feathers in drops.
terms.art: A duck turning its head back to rub its beak near its tail.

terms.meaning: A tree that grows in salty mud on sea coasts, where the tide comes in and out every day.
terms.example: The Pichavaram mangrove forest in Tamil Nadu has narrow water paths between its trees.
terms.art: Mangrove trees standing on tangled roots in shallow sea water, with a small boat between them.

terms.meaning: Roots that grow upwards out of the mud, so the plant can take in air. Mud under water has very little air in it.
terms.example: Around some mangrove trees, hundreds of pencil-like roots poke up out of the mud.
terms.art: Many thin roots sticking straight up out of grey mud around a mangrove tree.

terms.meaning: One step in a family line: parents are one generation, their children the next.
terms.example: You, your parents and your grandparents are three generations.
terms.art: A grandmother, a mother and a child standing in a row, from tallest to shortest.

explanations.definition: An adaptation is a feature of a living thing's body, or a way it behaves, that helps it live and have young in its habitat. It is passed down from parents to young.
explanations.description: Every habitat has its own problems. A desert has little water and burning days. A snowy mountain is freezing. A pond means living in water. A cave is completely dark. To understand any adaptation, first ask: what is this living thing's problem here? Then ask: how does this feature help with it? A camel's problem is that water is scarce. Its body loses very little water, so it can go for days without drinking. Some adaptations are parts of the body, like a duck's webbed feet. Some are ways of behaving, like a desert lizard hiding in its burrow at noon. An adaptation is different from acclimatising. If you move from Kochi to a hot, dry Delhi summer, your body starts to sweat sooner within a week or two. That change happens in your own life, and it is not passed on to your children. A camel's way of saving water is built into every camel calf.
examples: A cactus stores water in its fat stem. Its problem is that rain comes rarely.
A snow leopard has thick fur. Its problem is the freezing cold of the mountains.
A desert lizard hides under the sand at noon. That is a way of behaving that keeps it from overheating.
explanations.art: Four panels, each with a problem and an answer: a dry desert and a fat cactus, a snowy rock and a furry snow leopard, a pond and a duck's webbed foot, a dark cave and a pale fish with no eyes.
explanations.context: What is an adaptation? This card explains the word, and how to understand any adaptation by asking about the living thing's problem first.

explanations.concept: Keeping water in a hot, dry place: plants
explanations.definition: Water evaporates from a plant into dry air, mostly through its leaves. Desert plants lose water slowly because they have little surface for their size, a thick waxy coat, and stomata that open mostly at night.
explanations.description: A plant's problem in a desert is that rain may come only a few times a year, while the hot, dry air pulls water out of it every day. Water can only escape through a plant's outside, where it touches the air. A big, thin leaf has a lot of outside, so it loses water fast. A cactus has no flat leaves at all. Its leaves are spines, and its stem is fat and round. That shape holds a lot of water with little outside, just like the rolled-up towel in this unit's experiment. Its stem is covered with a thick waxy coat, which water hardly passes through. Its stomata, the tiny holes that let air in and water out, open mostly at night, when the air is cooler and less water escapes. Aloe vera stores water in thick, juicy leaves. Other desert plants solve the problem differently. The khejri tree of the Thar Desert, the state tree of Rajasthan, sends its roots very deep to reach water far underground. Some grasses, and rice in a dry spell, roll their leaves into thin tubes in the hot afternoon and open them again in the evening.
examples: The spines of a cactus are its leaves. They also protect the juicy stem from thirsty animals.
Rub a cabbage leaf with your finger and you feel a smooth wax. Many plants have a waxy coat, but desert plants have the thickest.
When paddy leaves roll up at midday in a dry spell, farmers know the plants are short of water.
explanations.art: A fat, round cactus with spines next to a broad, thin banana leaf, with small arrows of water vapour leaving the banana leaf from all over, and only a few leaving the cactus.
explanations.context: How do plants in deserts keep their water? This card explains, using shape, a waxy coat and tiny holes in the leaves.

explanations.concept: Keeping cool and saving water: desert animals
explanations.definition: Desert animals keep cool and save water by hiding from the midday heat, by losing little water from their bodies, and by getting rid of heat through big ears and thin parts of the body.
explanations.description: Sweating cools a body, because sweat takes heat away as it evaporates. But in a desert, every drop of sweat is water an animal may not be able to replace. So desert animals have other ways. The camel lets its body warm up by several degrees during a hot day, instead of sweating to stay cool. At night it cools down again. Its thick fur on its back shades its skin from the sun. Its hump is a store of fat, not water. It can close its nostrils against blowing sand, and its long eyelashes keep sand out of its eyes. Many small desert animals, like gerbils, lizards and beetles, spend the hot day in burrows under the sand, where it is cooler, and come out at night or at dawn. Desert foxes have big ears. Blood flows close to the thin skin of the ears, and heat leaves the blood into the air. A fennec fox of the Sahara has the biggest ears for its size of any fox. An Arctic fox has small ears, which lose little heat.
examples: A camel can lose water equal to about a quarter of its body weight and still recover when it drinks. Most mammals would die long before that.
Many desert animals get most of their water from their food, like seeds, leaves and the insects they eat.
Indian desert gerbils dig burrows and stay inside them through the hottest hours.
explanations.art: A camel lying in the sand at noon, a fennec fox with huge ears in the shade of a bush, and a cut-away of a cool burrow under the dunes with a gerbil inside.
explanations.context: How do animals live in the heat of a desert, with little water? This card explains how the camel, the desert fox and burrowing animals do it.

explanations.definition: A warm body loses heat through its outside, into the cold air or water. Cold-place animals keep their warmth with thick fur or feathers, a layer of fat, small ears and tails, and by curling up or huddling together.
explanations.description: A snow leopard's body is warm inside, and the air around it in winter can be far below freezing. Heat always moves from a warm place to a cold place. So the snow leopard's problem is that heat escapes from its body all the time, through its skin. Its thick fur is insulation. The fur traps still air between its hairs, and the still air slows the heat down. Its long, thick tail is almost as long as its body. When it rests, it wraps the tail round its body and face like a scarf. Its wide, furry paws spread its weight on the snow, and fur under the paws keeps them warm. Its ears are small and round, so little heat escapes from them. Yaks in Ladakh have long, shaggy hair that hangs almost to the ground, with soft wool underneath. Changthangi goats on the cold Changthang plateau of Ladakh grow a fine, soft underwool in winter. People comb it out in spring and spin it into pashmina. Whales and seals have blubber, a thick layer of fat under the skin. Curling up and huddling help too. A dog sleeping on a cold night curls into a ball and tucks its nose under its tail. Emperor penguins in the Antarctic winter crowd together in a huddle. The middle of a huddle can be warmer than 20 degrees Celsius while the wind outside is far below freezing. The birds keep shuffling, so each one takes turns on the cold outside.
examples: Pigeons puff up their feathers on a cold morning. The thicker coat traps more still air.
In the huddle test in this unit, ice cubes huddled together melted more slowly than ice cubes spread apart.
Mountain animals, like the Himalayan marmot, sleep through the coldest months in burrows. This deep winter sleep is called hibernation.
explanations.art: A snow leopard asleep on a snowy rock with its long thick tail wrapped round its face, and behind it a crowd of emperor penguins huddled in a blizzard.
explanations.context: How do animals keep warm in icy places? This card explains fur, fat, small ears, curling up and huddling.

explanations.definition: Some living things survive being frozen. Some frogs freeze solid in winter and thaw in spring. Many mountain plants grow low and close to the ground, out of the icy wind.
explanations.description: Ice is a danger for a living thing, because sharp ice crystals can break its cells. Most animals must keep warm to avoid freezing. A few do something surprising instead. The wood frog of North America lets itself freeze in winter. Its heart stops beating and it stops breathing. About two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice. Before it freezes, its liver floods its body with sugar. The sugar keeps the inside of its cells from freezing and breaking. In spring it thaws, its heart starts again, and it hops away. The Canadian scientists Kenneth and Janet Storey studied these frogs for many years. High in the Himalaya, many plants grow as low, tight cushions or flat rosettes pressed against the ground. Near the ground, the wind is weaker and the sun warms the soil, so the plant stays warmer than the air just above it.
examples: Some insects in cold places make their own antifreeze, a substance that stops their body water from freezing.
Pine trees in snowy places have thin, waxy needles and sloping branches, so heavy snow slides off without breaking them.
explanations.art: A frozen frog lying under fallen leaves in snow, and next to it the same frog in spring sunshine, hopping away.
explanations.context: Can a living thing freeze and still live? This card is about frogs that freeze solid, and plants that hug the ground.

explanations.definition: Water animals and plants have features that help them breathe, move, stay afloat and keep dry or warm in water.
explanations.description: Water is a very different place from air. It is hard to push through, it holds much less oxygen than air, and it can be salty. A fish breathes with gills. Water flows in through its mouth and out over its gills, which take oxygen from the water. Its body is streamlined, smooth and narrow, so water slides past it. Its fins push and steer. Ducks have webbed feet. The skin between their toes pushes against the water like a paddle. When the foot comes forward, the toes fold together, so it does not push the duck back. A duck spreads oil from its preen gland over its feathers, so water runs off in drops instead of soaking in. Water plants have problems too. The water hyacinth floats because its leaf stalks are swollen and spongy, full of air. A lotus stem, sold in markets as kamal kakdi or thamarai thandu, is full of holes when you cut it. These are air channels that carry air down to the parts under the mud. Mangrove trees grow in salty mud on the coast. The mud under water has very little air, so some mangroves send up breathing roots out of the mud. Some, like the grey mangrove, push the extra salt out through their leaves. On a dry day you can sometimes see salt crystals on the leaves.
examples: The mudskipper is a fish that lives in mangroves. It can climb out of the water on its fins, and breathes through its skin and the lining of its mouth while it is out.
Otters have webbed feet and thick fur that traps a layer of air, so the water does not reach their skin.
Dolphins and whales breathe air, so their nostril, the blowhole, is on the top of their head.
explanations.art: Under water: a streamlined fish with its fins, a duck's webbed foot paddling, a cut lotus stem showing its holes, and mangrove roots poking up from the mud.
explanations.context: How are living things suited to water? This card explains gills, fins, webbed feet, oily feathers and air-filled plants.

explanations.definition: Animals that live at night, in caves or in the deep sea find their way and their food with very big eyes, eyes that shine, long whiskers, sound and touch.
explanations.description: There are three main kinds of dark place. Night comes to every habitat. Caves are dark all the time. The deep sea, below about 1,000 metres, never gets any sunlight. The problem is the same in all three: how do you find food, and avoid being eaten, when you can hardly see? Many night animals have huge eyes that collect as much light as possible. The slender loris of the forests of South India and Sri Lanka has enormous round eyes for its small face. Owls have eyes so big that they cannot move them in their sockets. Instead, an owl turns its whole head, up to about three quarters of a full turn. Many night animals, like cats, cows and crocodiles, have a shiny layer at the back of the eye. It reflects light back through the eye, so the light gets a second chance to be caught. This is what makes their eyes shine in a torch beam. Other animals use other senses. A cat's whiskers feel the air and the walls. A barn owl can catch a mouse in total darkness by sound alone. The American scientist Roger Payne showed this by letting a barn owl hunt in a completely dark room. Small insect-eating bats and dolphins use echolocation. Many deep-sea fish make their own light.
examples: The Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal, lives in muddy water where it can hardly see. Its eyes have no lens, so it can probably tell only light from dark. It finds fish by echolocation.
The big fruit bats you see hanging in trees in Indian cities find their food mostly with their eyes and noses. Most of them do not echolocate.
A fish's lateral line feels the water move, so it can sense another fish swimming nearby in the dark.
explanations.art: A night scene: a slender loris with huge eyes on a branch, an owl turning its head, a cat's eyes shining in a torch beam, and a bat sending out sound waves towards a moth.
explanations.context: How do animals find their way and their food in the dark? This card explains big eyes, eyeshine, whiskers and echolocation.

explanations.concept: Cave fish: why did they lose their eyes?
explanations.description: In about thirty caves in Mexico live pale, blind fish. They are the same kind of fish, the Mexican tetra, as the silvery fish with good eyes that swim in the rivers outside. Their eyes start to grow when the baby fish is forming, then shrink and get covered with skin. They also have more taste buds and bigger lateral line sensors than the river fish. In India, cave explorers found large, pale fish in a cave in the Jaintia Hills of Meghalaya in 2019. Scientists described them as a new kind of fish in 2023. Why do fish that live in the dark lose their eyes? Scientists have several ideas, and they still argue about how much each one matters.
examples: In a completely dark cave, eyes cannot help a fish find food.
Cave fish from different caves lost their eyes separately, through changes in different genes.
Keeping eyes and the parts of the brain that see working uses a lot of energy, and caves have little food.

perspectives.who: Many scientists who study cave fish
perspectives.explanation: Eyes cost energy to keep working, and caves have very little food. Fish that spent less energy on useless eyes had more energy left for growing and having young. Over many generations, fish with smaller eyes did better.

perspectives.who: Other scientists, such as William Jeffery, who studied the Mexican cave fish for many years
perspectives.explanation: The same changes in the young fish's body that give it more taste buds and better jaw sensors also make its eyes shrink. Fish that were better at finding food by taste and touch did better, and they lost their eyes as a side effect.
In the dark, a fish with a broken eye gene is no worse off than one with good eyes. So changes that break eye genes are not weeded out. They simply build up over many generations.

explanations.art: Two fish side by side: a silvery river fish with big eyes, and a pale pink cave fish with no eyes, in a dark cave pool.
explanations.context: Fish that live in dark caves often have no eyes. This card is about why, which scientists still discuss.

explanations.description: A camel calf is born with a body that saves water. Nobody taught it. So how did camels come to be like this? People have given different answers. Today, almost all biologists agree that body features like a camel's are passed down in families, and that they built up over very many generations. They still discuss some of the details.
examples: Children look a little like their parents, but no two are exactly alike. Living things in the same family vary.

In the 1880s, the German scientist August Weismann cut the tails off mice, generation after generation. Every new baby mouse was still born with a full tail. A change made to a parent's body was not passed on.
A lizard decides every day when to sit in the sun and when to hide in the shade. Behaviour can change within a day.

perspectives.who: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a French scientist, in 1809
perspectives.explanation: Animals change their bodies by using them. A giraffe that stretches for leaves gets a slightly longer neck, and passes that longer neck on to its young. Most scientists now say this is wrong for body features like necks. Weismann's mice were one test against it.

perspectives.who: Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace, two British scientists, in 1858
perspectives.explanation: Young living things vary a little, and they inherit features from their parents. In a desert, the ones that happen to lose less water are more likely to survive and have young. Over many generations, the whole group comes to save water better. This is called natural selection.

Living things are not only shaped by their habitat. They also choose where to live and how to act, and they change their habitats. A beaver builds a dam, and earthworms change the soil. Those choices and changes decide which features help. Scientists call this niche construction.

explanations.art: A family tree of camels going back many generations, each one a little different, with the hot sun above them all.
explanations.context: How did camels, cactuses and snow leopards come to be suited to their homes? This card gives the main answers people have given.

explanations.concept: The same problem, the same answer
explanations.definition: Living things that are not closely related often end up with similar adaptations when they live in similar places. Scientists call this convergent evolution.
explanations.description: Cactuses grow wild in the Americas. Some euphorbias grow in the dry parts of Africa and India. They come from very different plant families. Yet both have fat, green, spiny stems and almost no leaves. The same problem, keeping water in the desert, led to the same shape twice. Look at a shark and a dolphin. A shark is a fish. A dolphin is a mammal, like a cow or you, and breathes air. Yet both have a streamlined body, a fin on the back and a strong tail, because both must swim fast through water. In caves all over the world, from Mexico to Meghalaya, fish, shrimps and beetles have turned pale and lost their eyes.
examples: A fat, spiny euphorbia hedge in an Indian village can look so like a cactus that most people call it one. Break a stem carefully and look: a euphorbia has white, milky sap. Its sap stings eyes and skin, so only a grown-up should do this.
Penguins and dolphins both swim with flippers, though one is a bird and the other a mammal.
explanations.art: A cactus and a spiny euphorbia standing side by side, and below them a shark and a dolphin swimming in the same direction with the same shape.
explanations.context: Why do living things that are not related sometimes look alike? This card explains that the same problem can lead to the same answer.

explanations.definition: An adaptation that helps in one place can be a problem in another. Each living thing is suited to its own habitat, not to every habitat.
explanations.description: A yak's thick, shaggy coat keeps it warm in Ladakh. Down in the plains in summer, the same coat would make it dangerously hot. A cave fish without eyes does well in the dark, but in a sunny river it could not see a bird coming to catch it. An owl's huge eyes are excellent at night, but they cannot move in their sockets. A cactus grows slowly, partly because opening its stomata only at night lets in less air to make food. So no living thing is best everywhere. Each one fits its own place.
examples: A polar bear in a hot zoo needs cold water and shade, because its fur and fat hold in so much heat.
A snow leopard's thick fur would make it far too hot in the forests of Kerala.
explanations.art: A yak looking hot and unhappy on a sunny plain, next to the same yak happy on a snowy mountain.
explanations.context: Is there a living thing that is suited to everywhere? This card explains why each adaptation fits one place and costs something.

explanations.concept: People adapt mostly with what they make
explanations.definition: People live in deserts, on icy mountains, on boats and in the dark. Mostly we do it with clothes, homes, fire and tools, and with knowledge passed from person to person.
explanations.description: Our bodies have some adaptations of their own. We sweat a lot, which helps us keep cool while running in the heat. Our bodies also acclimatise. After a week or two of hot weather, a person starts to sweat sooner. But people do not grow fur in Ladakh. They wear thick woollen clothes and build thick-walled homes with windows facing the winter sun. In Thar Desert villages, many homes have thick mud walls and thatched roofs, which keep the inside cooler than the air by day. In coastal Kerala and Tamil Nadu, roofs slope steeply so the heavy monsoon rain runs off. A camel's adaptations took many generations to build up. A new idea for a house can spread across a village in a year.
examples: Woollen clothes borrow the sheep's adaptation, a coat of trapped air.
A torch at night does the job that huge eyes do for a slender loris.
explanations.art: Three homes side by side: a flat-roofed Ladakhi house with a sunny window, a thick-walled mud hut with a thatched roof in the Thar, and a steep tiled roof in rainy Kerala.
explanations.context: How do people live in hot, cold and wet places? This card explains how we mostly adapt with what we make.

agreed.text: Living things have features of body and behaviour that suit them to their habitats. These are called adaptations.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have studied thousands of living things in deserts, snow, water and caves, and measured how their features help them.

agreed.text: Water and heat leave a body through its outside, so shape, size and coverings change how fast they escape.
agreed.evidence: Wet towels of the same size dry at different speeds when rolled, covered or spread out. Scientists have measured how fur, feathers and fat slow heat loss in animals.

agreed.text: A camel's hump is a store of fat, not water.
agreed.evidence: Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen studied camels in the Sahara in the 1950s, and others have checked their work since.

agreed.text: Adaptations of the body are passed from parents to young, and build up over many generations.
agreed.evidence: Young camels are born with bodies that save water. Breeders, and scientists studying fish, birds and plants, have watched features change over generations.

agreed.text: Similar places often give unrelated living things similar shapes.
agreed.evidence: Cactuses and euphorbias, sharks and dolphins, and cave animals all over the world show the same answers to the same problems.

challenging.claim: A camel stores water in its hump.
challenging.who: A very common idea, in many countries
challenging.for: A camel can go many days without drinking, and the hump looks like a tank.
challenging.against: The hump is mostly fat. A camel saves water by losing very little: it lets its body warm up by day instead of sweating, and loses little water in its droppings and urine. Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen showed this in the 1950s.
challenging.context: Is a camel's hump full of water? This card looks at a very common idea.

challenging.claim: An animal grows a new feature because it needs one. A giraffe's neck grew long because giraffes stretched for leaves.
challenging.who: Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, in 1809, and many people today
challenging.for: Using a body part can make it stronger in your own life. Muscles grow with exercise.
challenging.against: Changes made to a parent's body in its own life are not passed on to its young in that way. August Weismann cut the tails off mice for many generations, and their babies always had tails. Long necks built up because giraffes with slightly longer necks survived and had more young.
challenging.context: Does an animal grow a feature because it needs it? This card looks at an old idea.

challenging.claim: Animals of the same kind are bigger in colder places.
challenging.who: Carl Bergmann, a German scientist, in 1847
challenging.for: A big body has less outside for its size than a small one, so it loses heat more slowly. Many birds and mammals are bigger in colder places.
challenging.against: Many animals do not follow this rule. Food, enemies and other things also change body size. Scientists still argue about how often it holds and why.
challenging.context: Are animals bigger where it is colder? This card looks at a rule some scientists still argue about.

challenging.claim: A polar bear's see-through hairs carry sunlight down to its black skin, like glass tubes, to warm it.
challenging.who: An idea once printed in many books and articles
challenging.for: A polar bear's hairs really are clear and hollow, and its skin really is black.
challenging.against: In 1998, the American scientist Daniel Koon tested polar bear hairs in the lab. They hardly carried light along at all. The fur looks white because the clear hairs scatter light, and it keeps the bear warm mostly by trapping still air.
challenging.context: Do polar bear hairs carry sunlight to the skin? This card looks at an idea that turned out wrong.

challenging.who: A common saying, 'as blind as a bat'
challenging.for: Many bats find their food in the dark by echolocation, not by sight.
challenging.against: Every kind of bat can see. The big fruit bats of Indian cities find their food mostly with their eyes and noses.
challenging.context: Are bats blind? This card looks at a common saying.

challenging.claim: An owl can turn its head all the way round.
challenging.for: Owls turn their heads much further than we can, because their eyes cannot move in their sockets.
challenging.against: An owl can turn its head up to about three quarters of a full turn, not a full turn.
challenging.context: Can an owl turn its head right round? This card looks at what owls can really do.

big_questions.q: Your flat towel and your rolled towel held the same water. Why did one dry so much faster?
big_questions.hint: Where does the water leave from? How much of each towel touched the air?

big_questions.q: Ice cubes in a huddle melted more slowly than ice cubes spread apart. Does a huddle of penguins lose its warmth more slowly for the same reason?
big_questions.hint: Think about which parts of each cube or penguin touch the outside.

big_questions.q: A cave fish has no eyes, but it finds food in the dark. Is it missing something, or does it have something we lack?
big_questions.hint: Think about what its taste buds and lateral line can do.

big_questions.q: A camel calf is born already able to save water. Who or what 'designed' it?
big_questions.hint: Think about its parents, and their parents, going back many generations in the desert.

big_questions.q: If you could have one adaptation from another animal, which would you choose, and what problem of yours would it solve?
big_questions.hint: Start with the problem: heat, cold, water or darkness?

big_questions.q: A bat hears its world, a fish feels its world through the water, and you see yours. Is it the same world for all three?
big_questions.hint: Each of them meets the same pond or cave through a different sense.

big_questions.q: People go to Ladakh in woollen clothes, while a yak grows its own coat. Is a coat you make yourself different from a coat you grow?
big_questions.hint: One is passed on by teaching, the other by being born.

big_questions.q: No living thing is best everywhere. Is that true of people too?
big_questions.hint: Think of someone who is good at something you are not.

story.title: Twenty Pots and One Bucket
story.note: In the summer of 2019, the lakes that supply Chennai really did nearly dry up, and many buildings got their water by lorry. Rice leaves really do roll up in a dry spell and open again in the evening. Gardeners really do group pots together and cover the soil with dry leaves to save water in hot weather. Kavya, her Paati, her Thatha and their terrace are imagined.
text: In the summer of 2019, the lakes that gave Chennai its water almost dried up. Water came to Kavya's building in a blue lorry, three mornings a week. Every bucket was counted.

Kavya was nine. She lived on the fourth floor in Mylapore with her Paati, her grandmother. On the terrace above them, Paati kept twenty pots. There was tulsi, jasmine, curry leaf, a red hibiscus and two chilli plants. In the far corner stood one fat, spiny plant that nobody ever watered on purpose. Paati called it kalli.
Then Paati's sister in Madurai fell ill, and Paati had to go to her for a week. Before she left, she put one steel bucket on the terrace.
'This is the terrace's water for two days,' she said. 'Not one mug more. The building needs every drop.'
'But twenty pots, Paati!'
'Then use your head,' said Paati, and she squeezed Kavya's hand and went down the stairs with her bag.

The next morning, Kavya gave every pot the same mug of water. By eleven o'clock the sun was a white blaze over the water tank. When she went up at noon, the tulsi was drooping. Its leaves hung down like wet cloth. The jasmine leaves had curled at the edges. The soil in the pots by the parapet was already pale and dry on top.
Only the kalli looked exactly the same as it had at breakfast.
Kavya sat in the strip of shade by the water tank and phoned her Thatha. He grew paddy near Thanjavur, and he knew everything about dry weather.
'In a dry spell,' Thatha said, 'my paddy leaves roll up into thin tubes at midday. They look like green needles. In the evening, when it cools, they open out flat again.'
'Why do they roll up?'
'To hide from the sun,' he said. 'A flat leaf in the sun dries out. A rolled leaf keeps its water.' Then he had to go, because a cow was in the wrong field.

Kavya went to look at the kalli. She had never really looked at it before. It had no flat leaves at all. Its stems were thick, round and green, like a bundle of fat green pencils. She pressed one with her fingernail. It was hard and smooth, as if someone had polished it. Then she touched a tulsi leaf. It was thin and soft, and wide for how thin it was.

She thought about the washing on their balcony downstairs. A shirt pegged out flat was dry by lunch. A shirt left bundled in the bucket was still damp at night. The bundled shirt had the same water in it. It just had less of itself out in the air.
'So the water leaves from the outside,' Kavya said out loud, to a pigeon on the parapet. 'If I can't give the plants more water, I have to make them lose less.'
She could not roll up a tulsi plant. But she could do something else.

She dragged the pots, one by one, into the shade of the water tank. She pushed them close together, so their leaves touched. She put the tall hibiscus and the curry leaf on the sunny side, and the drooping tulsi right in the middle. The pots in the middle were hidden from the sun and the hot wind by the pots around them.

Then she went down to the building's dustbin area, where the gardener swept the dry neem leaves into a heap. She filled a bag with them. She spread a thick layer of dry leaves over the soil in every pot, like a blanket.
It took her the whole afternoon. She was sunburnt and sweaty and her arms ached. But when she checked at five o'clock, the tulsi in the middle was standing up again.

The next day was even hotter. At noon, Kavya went up the stairs two at a time. The crowd of pots was green. The tulsi was upright. She pushed a finger under the leaf blanket in one pot. The soil underneath was dark and cool and damp.

Only one pot looked unhappy. It was a small chilli plant she had forgotten, left alone by the parapet in the full sun. Its leaves hung limp. Kavya carried it into the crowd and gave it half a mug from the bucket.
The bucket lasted two whole days. So did the next one.
When Paati came back on Sunday, she stopped at the top of the stairs and stared at the huddle of pots by the water tank.
'Who moved my garden?'
'I did,' said Kavya. 'The plants keep each other's water now. The ones in the middle hardly feel the sun. And the leaves on the soil stop it drying out.'
Paati walked slowly round the crowd of pots, touching the leaves. Then she laughed. 'My mother did the same thing in Madurai, every May,' she said. 'I had forgotten.'
She looked over at the corner, where the kalli still stood alone in the full sun, fat and spiny and perfectly fine.
'And that one?' she asked.
'That one never needed help,' said Kavya. 'It has no thin leaves to lose water from. It keeps all its water inside a fat, waxy stem.'
That night, Kavya wrote in her notebook in big letters. Water leaves through the outside. Less outside, less water lost. Then, underneath, smaller: Ask Thatha how the paddy knows when to roll up.
story.epiphany: For the parent: water escapes from a plant through its surface, where it touches the hot, dry air. Kavya could not give the plants more water, so she cut the surface they lost water from. Pots crowded together shade each other and hide from the hot wind, the way huddled penguins or ice cubes hide most of their outsides. The dry leaves on the soil work like a waxy coat, slowing the water escaping from the soil. Rolled paddy leaves and the fat, waxy stem of the kalli, a euphorbia, are the plants' own ways of having less outside for the water they hold.
ask: Why did the tulsi droop by noon, while the kalli did not?
What did Thatha tell Kavya about the paddy leaves? Why do they roll up?
How did the washing on the balcony help Kavya work out what to do?
Why did the pots in the middle of the crowd stay greener than the chilli plant by the parapet?
What did the layer of dry leaves do for the soil?

games.title: Survive the Place
games.context: This is a card game about adaptations. Players draw a place card with a problem, and must play a feature card that solves it, saying how it helps.

printables.title: 8 place cards
items: THAR DESERT, NOON: burning hot sun
THAR DESERT: no rain for months
POND: you must move through water
MANGROVE: salty mud with little air
FOREST AT NIGHT: dark, food is hiding

printables.title: 24 feature cards
items: Body that warms up by day instead of sweating
Long tail to wrap round you

rules: Shuffle the feature cards. Deal 5 to each player. Put the place cards face down in a pile.
Turn over the top place card and read it aloud.
Each player may play one feature card that helps with that place. To score, say the problem first, then how the feature helps. For example: 'It is burning hot, so big ears let heat escape.'
A good explanation scores 2 points. If the others agree the feature helps but the explanation is unclear, score 1 point.
After each place, everyone draws back up to 5 cards.
When all 8 places have been played, the player with the most points wins.
Playing alone: deal yourself 8 cards. Score a point for every place you can survive with your cards, and try to beat your score next time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out and shuffle the cards. 2. Deal 5 feature cards to each player. 3. Put the place cards face down.
flow.say: Each place has a problem. Your feature cards are adaptations. Play one that solves the problem, and say how.
flow.kid: Shuffle the cards. Take 5 feature cards. Each place has a problem. Can you solve it?
flow.context: This is the first step of Survive the Place. You set up a card game where adaptations solve the problems of hard places.

flow.do: Play the first place card together as practice: 'CAVE: total darkness, always.'
flow.say: Practice round. Which feature would help in a cave that is always dark?
flow.kid: Practice round. A cave is always dark. Which card helps?

check.q: A cave is always dark. Which feature helps most?
options: Thick waxy coat
Lateral line
Hump of fat
check.why: A lateral line feels the water moving, so a cave fish can find food and avoid rocks without seeing. A waxy coat saves water, and a hump stores fat. Both help in a desert, not in the dark.

flow.do: Take turns turning over place cards and playing feature cards, until all 8 places are played.
flow.say: Remember: problem first, then how the feature helps.
flow.kid: Turn over a place. Play a card. Say the problem, then how it helps.
flow.parent: Some cards help in more than one place. Thick fur helps in Ladakh, and a camel's fur shades it from the desert sun too. If your child can explain it, give the points.

flow.do: Add up the points and talk about the hardest place.
flow.say: Which place was hardest to survive? Which features did you wish you had?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Which place was hardest?
flow.think: Is there one feature that would help in every place?

setup.caption: 1. Put the place cards face down. Deal 5 feature cards each.

setup.art: A child laying a 'Big ears' card on top of a 'Thar Desert, noon' card.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a place. Play a feature that solves its problem.

games.title: Huddle Up!
games.context: This is a moving game for three or more people. Everyone is an emperor penguin, keeping warm in a huddle and taking turns on the cold outside.

printables.title: 6 weather cards
items: Calm, cold night: stand still in the huddle
Strong wind from the left: the left side shuffles to the back
Strong wind from the right: the right side shuffles to the back
Blizzard: squeeze in tight and count to 10
Sunny morning: spread out and stretch
Egg check: everyone checks the egg on their feet

rules: Everyone is a penguin. Put a soft ball or a rolled sock on top of your feet. That is your egg. Never let it touch the ice, the floor.
One person is the weather and reads a weather card.
On a wind card, the penguins on that side shuffle round to the sheltered side of the huddle, without dropping their eggs.
A penguin who drops its egg becomes the weather.
Play until every card has been read twice.

flow.do: Everyone stands in a tight group with a rolled sock on their feet.
flow.say: Emperor penguin fathers keep the egg on their feet all winter, and huddle together. Let's be penguins.
flow.kid: You are a penguin. Put the sock egg on your feet. Stand close together.
flow.context: This is the first step of Huddle Up. You play penguins keeping warm in a huddle.

flow.do: The weather reads the cards one at a time, and the penguins move.
flow.say: Wind from the left! Left side, shuffle round to the back. Don't drop your egg!
flow.kid: Listen to the weather. Shuffle round when the wind comes. Keep your egg on your feet!
flow.parent: Shuffling with an egg on your feet is slow and wobbly, which is how real penguins move in a huddle. Keep it gentle, with no pushing.

flow.do: Stop and talk.
flow.say: Who felt warmest in a huddle: the penguins in the middle or on the outside? Why do penguins keep moving round?
flow.kid: Who would be warmest, in the middle or outside? Why do penguins take turns?

check.q: Why do real penguins keep shuffling round in a huddle?
options: So every penguin gets a turn in the warm middle
Because they are bored
To find food
check.why: The penguins on the outside face the icy wind and lose heat fastest. By shuffling, each penguin takes turns on the outside and in the warm middle. Scientists filming huddles saw the whole crowd move in small steps, like a slow wave. Picking 'to find food' is a fair guess, but there is no food on the ice. They find it in the sea.

setup.caption: 1. Stand close in a huddle, with a sock egg on your feet.

setup.art: The people on one side of the group shuffling round to the other side, while one person reads a card.
setup.caption: 2. When the wind comes, the outside penguins shuffle round.

experiments.title: Three Wet Leaves: which one keeps its water longest?
experiments.question: Three paper towels hold the same water. One is spread flat like a big thin leaf, one is rolled up like a fat cactus stem, and one is covered like a leaf with a waxy coat. Which keeps its water longest?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which towel will dry first, and which will stay wet longest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use three towels of the same size, wet them the same way, and put them on the same kind of plate in the same place. Only the shape and the covering change. Check all three at the same times.

materials.item: 3 paper kitchen towels of the same size. Or 3 same-sized pieces of thin old cotton cloth, such as an old hanky cut up.
a bowl of water
3 plates of the same kind, such as 3 steel plates
a piece of thin plastic cut from a clean, empty milk packet, or cling film, a little bigger than one towel
a pin, to make 5 tiny holes in the plastic
some small squares of dry tissue or newspaper, for the touch test
a fan or a sunny windowsill
a kitchen scale, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the pin holes and puts the pin away. Keep the bowl of water away from switches and sockets.

schedule.what: Set up three wet towels, flat, rolled and covered. Check them every 15 minutes for an hour or more, then unroll and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table every 15 minutes with wet, damp or dry. At the end, draw the three towels and colour in the parts that were still wet.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the three dry towels and the three plates. 2. Explain the three shapes. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Each towel will be a pretend leaf, holding the same water. One will be flat and open, one rolled up tight, and one covered with plastic. Which do you think will stay wet longest? Why?
flow.kid: You will make three pretend leaves. One flat. One rolled up. One covered. Which will stay wet longest? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which towel do you think will dry first, and why?
good: The flat one, because all of it is open to the air.
The rolled one, because it is fatter.
Any guess with a reason is good.

flow.parent: Write down your child's guess and reason before you start. Do not explain anything yet. The test will answer the question.
flow.context: This is the first step of the three wet leaves experiment. You guess which wet paper towel will keep its water longest: flat, rolled or covered.

flow.do: 1. Dip the first towel in the bowl until it is soaked. 2. Hold it up by one corner until it stops dripping. 3. Lay it on a plate. 4. Do the same with the other two.
flow.say: We wet them all the same way, so each towel starts with about the same water. Hold it up until the drips stop.
flow.kid: Dip a towel in the water. Hold it up until it stops dripping. Put it on a plate. Do all three the same way.
flow.parent: If you have a kitchen scale, weigh each plate with its wet towel now and write the numbers down. The weight lost later is the water that escaped. Paper towels tear when wet, so lift them gently by a corner.

flow.do: 1. Leave towel A spread out flat. 2. Roll towel B up tightly into a fat tube. 3. Leave towel C flat, and lay the plastic over it.
flow.say: Towel A is a big, thin leaf. Towel B is a fat cactus stem. Towel C is a leaf with a waxy coat, but with a few tiny holes.
flow.kid: Leave towel A flat. Roll towel B up tight, like a fat stem. Cover towel C with the plastic.
flow.parent: Before laying the plastic on towel C, a grown-up pokes 5 tiny pin holes in it, spread out. These are like the tiny holes in a real leaf, called stomata. Press the plastic down gently so it touches the towel all over, and tuck its edges under the towel.

flow.do: Put the three plates side by side, under the fan or on a sunny windowsill. Write down the time.
flow.say: All three go in the same place, so they get the same air and the same warmth. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Put the three plates side by side under the fan. Write down the time.

flow.do: 1. Every 15 minutes, press a dry tissue square on top of each towel for 3 seconds. 2. A wet patch on the tissue means the towel is still wet. 3. Write wet, damp or dry in the table.
flow.say: Let's do the touch test. A dark wet patch means water is still there. A faint patch means damp. No patch means dry.
flow.kid: Every 15 minutes, press a dry tissue on each towel. Is there a wet patch? Write wet, damp or dry.
flow.parent: Each check takes only a minute. In between, you can read the story or play a game. For towel C, lift one corner of the plastic, test, and press it back down. Under a fan in dry weather, the flat towel is usually dry in 45 to 90 minutes. In humid monsoon weather it can take 2 to 3 hours, so keep checking, or put the plates in a sunny window.

flow.do: 1. When the flat towel is dry, gently unroll towel B and lift the plastic off towel C. 2. Feel each one all over with your fingers. 3. Weigh them again if you can.
flow.say: Now let's look inside. Feel the middle of the rolled towel, and the towel under the plastic.
flow.kid: Unroll towel B. Lift the plastic off towel C. Feel them. Which parts are still wet?

check.q: The flat towel is dry, but the inside of the rolled towel is still wet. Why?
options: The rolled towel had more water to start with
Only the outside of the rolled towel touched the air, so water could only escape from there
Rolling paper makes water
check.why: Water evaporates only from a surface that touches the air. In the rolled towel, most of the paper was hidden inside the roll, so its water could not escape. Picking 'more water' is a fair worry. But we wet all three the same way, and a scale would show they started about the same.

flow.parent: You will usually find that the outer layer of the rolled towel is dry, but the middle is still wet. The covered towel is often wet all over, apart from tiny dry spots near the pin holes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a leaf loses water fastest when it is flat and open. What I saw: the flat towel was dry in an hour. The rolled one was still wet inside, and the covered one was wet nearly all over. Why: water escapes only where the towel touches the air. Rolling hides most of it, and the plastic covers it. That is why a cactus is fat and round, with a waxy coat.
flow.think: A cactus is fat and round with a waxy skin. Which of your three towels was most like a cactus?

experiments.context: In this experiment you make three pretend leaves from wet paper towels, flat, rolled and covered, and find out which keeps its water longest. It shows why desert plants are shaped the way they are.

experiments.title: The Huddle Test: do ice cubes melt more slowly together?
experiments.question: Emperor penguins huddle together in the cold. Do six ice cubes in a tight huddle melt more slowly than six cubes spread apart?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which group will melt faster, the huddle or the spread-out cubes, or will they melt at the same speed? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use 12 ice cubes from the same tray, two plates of the same kind, and the same place in the room. Only the way the cubes are arranged changes.
results_table: Huddled cubes: what they look like
Spread-out cubes: what they look like

materials.item: 12 ice cubes from the same tray
2 plates of the same kind, such as 2 steel thalis
2 glasses of the same size
a spoon
a clock or timer

experiments.safety: Wipe up melted water from the floor so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Put 6 ice cubes in a tight huddle and 6 spread apart. Check every 10 minutes for 30 minutes, then compare the meltwater.

experiments.record: Draw both plates at the start and after 30 minutes. Mark how high the meltwater came in each glass.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child about penguins huddling. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: In the Antarctic winter, emperor penguins crowd together in a huddle. We can't test penguins, but we can test ice. Will a huddle of ice melt faster, slower, or the same? Why?
flow.kid: Penguins huddle in the cold. Let's test ice cubes. Will huddled ice melt faster or slower? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the huddle test. You find out whether ice cubes melt more slowly when they are crowded together.

flow.do: 1. On plate A, push 6 cubes together into a tight block, 2 rows of 3. 2. On plate B, put 6 cubes apart, each a finger-width from the others. 3. Put both plates side by side, out of the sun.
flow.say: Plate A is the huddle. Plate B is six penguins standing alone. Both plates sit in the same place.
flow.kid: Push 6 cubes together into a block, 2 rows of 3. Spread the other 6 apart. Put the plates side by side.
flow.parent: Take all 12 cubes out of the tray at the same moment, so they start the same. Keep both plates out of direct sun and away from the fan, or the side nearest the fan will melt first.

flow.do: Every 10 minutes, look at both plates. Write down what you see: sharp corners, rounded corners, small cubes, or gone.
flow.say: Let's look again. Which cubes have lost their corners first? Which look smaller?
flow.kid: Every 10 minutes, look at both plates. Which cubes look smaller?
flow.parent: In a warm Indian room, the spread-out cubes usually look clearly smaller after 20 to 30 minutes. The huddle keeps its block shape longer. You can read the story or play a game while you wait.

flow.do: 1. After 30 minutes, hold the ice back with a spoon and pour the water from plate A into one glass. 2. Do the same for plate B into the other glass. 3. Compare.
flow.say: The water in each glass is the ice that melted. Which glass has more?
flow.kid: Hold the ice back with a spoon. Pour each plate's water into a glass. Which glass has more?

check.q: The spread-out cubes made more meltwater than the huddled cubes. Why?
options: The spread-out cubes were smaller to start with
Each spread-out cube had all its sides in the warm air, while in the huddle, many sides touched only other cold ice
Ice likes to be together
check.why: Heat from the warm air goes into ice through its outside. In the huddle, the sides of the cubes that touched each other were hidden from the warm air. So less heat got in. Picking 'smaller to start with' is a fair worry, but all the cubes came from the same tray. A penguin huddle works the same way in reverse. Less of each penguin's body faces the icy wind, so less heat escapes.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: things in a huddle swap less heat with the air around them. What I saw: after 30 minutes, the huddled cubes still had their block shape, and their glass had less water. Why: in the huddle, many sides of each cube were hidden from the warm air. That is why penguins huddle in the cold, and why a dog curls up on a cold night.

experiments.context: In this experiment you compare six ice cubes in a tight huddle with six cubes spread apart, to find out why penguins huddle in the cold.

experiments.title: The Jelly Coat: does a waxy skin keep a leaf fresh?
experiments.question: Desert plants have a thick waxy coat. If we give a leaf an extra coat, does it stay fresh for longer than a leaf without one?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will the coated leaf and the plain leaf wilt at the same speed, or will one stay fresh longer? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use two leaves of the same kind and size, picked at the same time. Put them side by side on the same plate. Only the coat changes.
results_table: Plain leaf: firm, a little limp, or floppy?
Coated leaf: firm, a little limp, or floppy?

materials.item: 2 fresh spinach (palak) leaves of the same size, with their stalks. Or 2 leaves from a potted plant, such as a money plant or hibiscus.
about half a teaspoon of petroleum jelly, which many homes keep for dry lips and skin
a plate
a fan or a sunny windowsill

experiments.safety: A grown-up picks any leaves from a potted plant, with clean scissors. Wash your hands after using the petroleum jelly. Do not eat the leaves afterwards.

schedule.what: Coat one leaf with petroleum jelly and leave it beside a plain leaf. Check them after 1, 3 and 5 hours.

experiments.record: Draw both leaves at the start and at the end. Write down when the plain leaf first went limp.

flow.do: 1. Show your child two leaves. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: We will give one leaf an extra waxy coat, and leave the other plain. Will one stay fresh longer? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: One leaf gets a coat. One stays plain. Which will stay fresh longer? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the jelly coat experiment. You find out whether a waxy coat keeps a leaf fresh.

flow.do: 1. Spread a thin layer of petroleum jelly over both sides of one leaf, with a fingertip. 2. Dab some on the cut end of its stalk too. 3. Leave the other leaf plain.
flow.say: The jelly is our pretend waxy coat, like the thick coat on a cactus. Spread it gently, so the leaf doesn't tear.
flow.kid: Spread a thin coat of jelly on both sides of one leaf. Dab some on the stalk end. Leave the other leaf plain.
flow.parent: A thin layer is enough. Hold the leaf flat on your palm and smooth the jelly outwards from the middle. The cut end of the stalk is where a picked leaf loses water fastest, so it needs a dab too.

flow.do: 1. Lay both leaves side by side on a plate, under the fan or on a sunny windowsill. 2. Hold each one up by its stalk. 3. Notice how firm it is now.
flow.say: Let's see how they stand now, at the start. Hold each one sideways by its stalk.
flow.kid: Hold each leaf sideways by its stalk. Does it stay straight? Put them on the plate.
flow.parent: Both leaves should stand out straight when held sideways by the stalk. That is how a leaf full of water behaves.

flow.do: After 1 hour, 3 hours and 5 hours, hold each leaf sideways by its stalk again. Write down: firm, a little limp, or floppy.
flow.say: Is it standing straight, bending a little, or hanging down?
flow.kid: Hold each leaf by its stalk again. Firm, a little limp, or floppy?
flow.wait: Check after 1 hour, 3 hours and 5 hours.

check.q: After 5 hours, the plain leaf hangs floppy but the coated leaf still stands out. Why?
options: The jelly fed the leaf
The jelly coat slowed down the water escaping from the leaf, so it kept its water
The coated leaf was a stronger leaf
check.why: A leaf is firm when its cells are full of water. Water escapes from a picked leaf through its surface and its tiny holes. The jelly covered them, so the coated leaf kept its water and stayed firm. Picking 'the jelly fed the leaf' is a natural guess, but petroleum jelly is not food for a plant. A cactus's thick waxy coat works the same way, all its life.

flow.parent: A spinach leaf under a fan usually goes limp within 2 to 4 hours. A thicker leaf, like money plant, can take a day, so check it the next morning instead. If both leaves stay firm, move the plate into the sun.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a waxy coat helps a leaf keep its water. What I saw: after a few hours the plain leaf was floppy, and the coated leaf was still firm. Why: the jelly covered the leaf's surface and its tiny holes, so less water escaped. Desert plants have a thick waxy coat of their own.

experiments.context: In this experiment you give one leaf a coat of petroleum jelly and leave another plain, to find out how a waxy coat helps desert plants keep their water.

activities.title: Feel the Ripple: sense the water like a fish in the dark

materials.item: a bucket or a big bowl, filled with water
a dupatta or scarf, for a blindfold
a steel spoon

activities.safety: Put the bucket on the floor on a towel. A grown-up stays close while your child's eyes are covered.

schedule.what: With eyes closed, hold a hand still in water and say when you feel the water move.

activities.record: Write down how far away the spoon was when you could still feel it: close, middle or far.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put one hand in the water, fingers spread, and keep it very still. 2. Cover their eyes with the dupatta.
flow.say: Fish have a row of tiny sensors along each side, called the lateral line. It feels the water move. Let's see what your hand can feel.
flow.kid: Put one hand in the water. Keep it very still. Close your eyes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Feel the Ripple. You find out how a fish can sense things moving in the dark, without seeing them.

flow.do: 1. Without touching your child, move the spoon quickly back and forth in the water, close to their hand. 2. Ask them to say 'now' when they feel it. 3. Try again further away, then further still.
flow.say: Say 'now' as soon as you feel anything. Can you tell which side it is coming from?
flow.kid: Say 'now' when you feel the water move. Which side is it on?
flow.parent: Move the spoon about 5 centimetres from the hand first, then about 15, then about 30. Wait a few seconds between tries, and sometimes wait without moving the spoon, so your child cannot just guess. Most children feel the push of the water at 5 centimetres, and some can tell which side it came from.

flow.do: Take off the blindfold and talk about what happened.
flow.say: A cave fish has no eyes. How do you think it swims round rocks and finds food in the dark?
flow.kid: A cave fish has no eyes. How does it find food in the dark?

check.q: How does a blind cave fish find its way in the dark?
options: It has a row of sensors along its sides that feel the water moving
It glows
It just bumps into things
check.why: A fish's lateral line feels the water moving around it, much as your hand felt the spoon's ripples. Moving animals, and water flowing past rocks, all make ripples. Picking 'it glows' mixes cave fish up with some deep-sea fish, which make their own light. Cave fish usually do not.

activities.context: This activity lets you feel the water move with your eyes closed, the way a fish's lateral line does, to understand how fish find their way in the dark.

activities.title: Whisker Walk: find your way without your eyes

materials.item: a dupatta or scarf, for a blindfold
a sheet of newspaper rolled into a long, thin stick, or a soft broom handle
a few cushions

activities.safety: Clear the floor of anything sharp or breakable. A grown-up walks right beside the child the whole time.

schedule.what: Walk along a hallway with eyes closed, first with hands only, then with a long newspaper whisker.

activities.record: Write which way was easier, and why.

flow.do: 1. Put 3 cushions on the floor along a short hallway or across a room. 2. Cover your child's eyes. 3. Walk beside them as they cross slowly, feeling with their hands.
flow.say: Cats, rats and seals have long whiskers that touch things before their faces do. First, let's try with just your hands.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Walk slowly across the room. Feel with your hands. Can you find the cushions?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Whisker Walk. You find out how whiskers help animals find their way in the dark.

flow.do: 1. Move the cushions to new places. 2. Give your child the rolled newspaper. 3. Let them sweep it slowly from side to side, just above the floor, as they cross again.
flow.say: Now you have a whisker. Sweep it gently from side to side. Does it find the cushions before your feet do?
flow.kid: Now use the paper whisker. Sweep it side to side. Does it find the cushions first?
flow.parent: Keep a hand near your child's shoulder. Stop them before they reach a wall or a door.

flow.do: Take off the blindfold and talk about it.
flow.say: Which way was easier? Why do you think a cat's whiskers are about as wide as its body?
flow.kid: Which way was easier? Why do cats have long whiskers?

ask.q: Why are a cat's whiskers about as wide as its body?
good: So it can tell if a gap is wide enough to get through.
So it feels things before it bumps into them.

flow.parent: Blind people who use a long white cane find their way in a similar way. The cane touches things well ahead of the feet.

activities.context: This activity is a walk with your eyes closed, first with only your hands and then with a long paper whisker, to understand how whiskers help animals at night.

activities.title: The Webbed Hand: paddle like a duck

materials.item: a bucket or a big bowl, filled with water
a thin, clean plastic bag, such as a vegetable bag

activities.safety: Plastic bags go only on hands, never near the face or head. A grown-up puts the bag away afterwards.

schedule.what: Push water with spread fingers, then with the hand inside a plastic bag that works like webbed skin.

activities.record: Write which push felt stronger, and draw a duck's foot.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to put one hand in the water with fingers spread wide apart. 2. Sweep it through the water from one side to the other. 3. Notice how hard it is to push.
flow.say: Sweep your spread fingers through the water. Does the water push back much?
flow.kid: Spread your fingers wide. Sweep your hand through the water. Does it push back?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Webbed Hand. You feel why ducks, frogs and otters have skin between their toes.

flow.do: 1. Put the plastic bag over the same hand like a loose glove, fingers still spread. 2. Sweep it through the water the same way.
flow.say: Now the bag fills the gaps between your fingers, like the skin on a duck's foot. How does the push feel now?
flow.kid: Put the bag on your hand like a glove. Spread your fingers. Sweep again. Is it harder?

check.q: Why is it harder to sweep the bag-covered hand through the water?
options: The bag is heavy
The bag fills the gaps between the fingers, so the hand pushes more water
Plastic is sticky in water
check.why: With spread fingers, water slips through the gaps. With the bag, the whole hand pushes against the water, like a paddle. Pushing more water back pushes the swimmer forward more. That is what a duck's webbed foot does. Picking 'heavy' is a fair guess, but a thin bag weighs almost nothing.

flow.do: Ask your child to sweep the bagged hand forward with the fingers closed together, then back with them spread.
flow.say: A duck folds its toes together when its foot comes forward, and spreads them to push back. Can you feel why?
flow.kid: Fingers together, move your hand forward. Fingers spread, push back. Which is easier?
flow.think: Why would it be bad for a duck to push water forward as hard as backward?

activities.context: This activity compares pushing water with spread fingers and with a plastic bag over the hand, to feel how webbed feet help ducks and frogs swim.

activities.title: Shining Eyes: why a cat's eyes glow in the dark

materials.item: 2 paper cups or small yoghurt cups of the same kind
a small square of aluminium foil
3 squares of black paper, each big enough to cover the top of a cup
tape or 2 rubber bands
a pencil, to poke a hole
a torch
a dark room

activities.safety: A grown-up pokes the holes with the pencil. Never shine a torch straight into anyone's eyes, or an animal's.

schedule.what: Make two model eyes, one with shiny foil at the back and one with black paper, and shine a torch at them in the dark.

activities.record: Draw both model eyes and colour the one that shone.

flow.do: 1. Put foil, shiny side up, in the bottom of one cup. 2. Put black paper in the bottom of the other. 3. Cover each cup's top with black paper and poke a pencil hole in the middle.
flow.say: These cups are model eyes. The hole is the pupil, where light goes in. One has a shiny layer at the back, like a cat's eye. The other is dark at the back, like yours.
flow.kid: Put foil in the bottom of one cup. Put black paper in the other. Cover both tops. Poke a hole in each.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shining Eyes. You make two model eyes to find out why some animals' eyes glow in a torch beam.
flow.parent: Tape the black paper tightly over the top of each cup, or hold it with a rubber band. The hole in the middle is the pupil. The bottom of the cup is the back of the eye.

flow.do: 1. Turn off the lights. 2. Lay both cups on their sides on a table, holes facing you. 3. Hold the torch just beside your own eyes and shine it at the holes from about one metre away.
flow.say: Which eye shines back at you?
flow.kid: Turn off the lights. Hold the torch beside your face. Shine it at both holes. Which one glows?
flow.parent: Hold the torch right next to your eyes, because the reflected light comes back towards the torch. If the foil eye does not glow, move the torch a little until the hole lines up with the foil inside. You should see a bright spot in the foil cup and only darkness in the black one.

check.q: Why does the foil eye shine, but not the black eye?
options: The foil makes its own light
The foil reflects the torch light back out through the hole
The black paper is broken
check.why: The foil does not make light. It bounces the torch's light back out through the hole. Many night animals, like cats, cows and crocodiles, have a shiny layer at the back of the eye that does the same. Light that passes through the eye once is bounced back for a second chance to be seen. That helps them see in dim light. Picking 'makes its own light' mixes eyeshine up with glow-worms and fireflies, which really do make light.

flow.do: Talk about where you might see eyeshine.
flow.say: At night, watch street cats and dogs in a car's headlights. Do their eyes shine? Do people's eyes shine like that?
flow.kid: Look out for shining eyes at night, from a safe place. Do people's eyes shine?
flow.parent: People's eyes do not have this shiny layer. The red eyes in some flash photos come from light bouncing off the blood-rich back of the eye, which is different.

activities.context: This activity makes two model eyes from cups, one with a shiny back like a cat's eye, to show why some animals' eyes glow at night.

activities.title: Leaf Coats in the Kitchen

materials.item: 4 or 5 different leaves from the kitchen or a potted plant: a cabbage leaf, spinach, curry leaves, coriander, and aloe vera if you have it
a spoon of water
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.safety: Wash your hands after touching aloe vera, and keep its jelly away from your eyes.

schedule.what: Drip water on different leaves and feel their surfaces, to find which have the thickest waxy coat.

activities.record: Make a table: leaf, thick or thin, do drops bead up or spread out?

flow.do: 1. Lay the leaves on a plate. 2. Ask your child to drip a few drops of water onto each one. 3. Watch whether the drops sit up as beads or spread out flat.
flow.say: Drops sit up as round beads on a waxy leaf, because water doesn't stick to wax. Which leaves have a waxy coat?
flow.kid: Drip water on each leaf. Do the drops stay round, or spread out flat?
flow.context: This is the first step of Leaf Coats. You look for the waxy coat on leaves from your kitchen.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to rub each leaf gently between finger and thumb. 2. Sort the leaves into thick and waxy, and thin and soft.
flow.say: Which leaves feel smooth and waxy? Which are thin and soft? Which do you think would last longest in the desert?
flow.kid: Rub each leaf gently. Smooth and waxy, or thin and soft? Which would last in a desert?

ask.q: Which leaf would last longest in the desert, and why?
good: The aloe, because it is thick and stores water.
The cabbage, because its drops beaded up, so it has a waxy coat.

flow.parent: Cabbage leaves show the waxy coat best: drops roll into shiny beads. Coriander and spinach leaves are thin and wilt quickly. Aloe vera is thick, juicy and waxy, a real succulent from dry places.

activities.context: This activity looks for the waxy coat on everyday leaves, by dripping water on them and feeling them.
