activities.title: Design an Animal for a Place

materials.item: paper and colour pencils

schedule.what: Pick a place and draw a made-up animal or plant that could live there, labelling each feature with the problem it solves.

activities.record: Your labelled drawing, with each feature's problem written beside it.

flow.do: Read out the five places and let your child pick one. The places are the Thar at noon, a Ladakh winter night, a mangrove, a cave and the deep sea.
flow.say: Pick a place. What problems would a living thing have there? Let's list them first.
flow.kid: Pick a place: desert, snowy mountain, mangrove, cave or deep sea. What problems would you have there?
flow.context: This is the first step of Design an Animal. You invent a living thing for one of the hard places in this unit.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to write down three problems of that place. 2. Then draw an animal or plant with one feature for each problem. 3. Label each feature with its problem.
flow.say: Start with the problem, then the feature. For the desert: little water, so what could your animal have?
flow.kid: Write three problems of your place. Draw a creature with a feature for each. Label them.
flow.parent: Good drawings name the problem first: 'It is very cold, so it has thick fur and a short tail.' Any made-up feature is fine if your child can say how it helps. Ask what it would cost: thick fur would be too hot in summer.

flow.do: Ask your child to show the drawing and explain one feature.
flow.say: Tell me about one feature. What problem does it solve? Is there a real animal with something like it?
flow.kid: Show your creature. Explain one feature. Does a real animal have something like it?

activities.context: This activity is drawing a made-up living thing for a hard place, like a desert or a cave, starting with the problems of that place.

projects.title: My Adaptation Notebook: ten living things near home

materials.item: a notebook and pencil
a window or balcony to watch from
the vegetable and fish shop, or the vegetables in your kitchen

projects.safety: Watch birds and animals from a window or balcony, and never touch or feed street animals without a grown-up.

schedule.what: From a window or balcony, find four living things, such as a crow, a pigeon, a potted plant and ants. Write one feature of each and the problem it solves.
In the kitchen or at the shop, find three more, such as a fish, a lotus stem or a cabbage. Write one feature of each.
Add three living things from books or this unit, from hot, cold, water and dark places. Make a page for each and share your notebook.

projects.record: One page for each living thing: its name, a drawing, its problem, its feature, and how the feature helps.

flow.do: 1. Sit at a window or on a balcony for 10 minutes. 2. Ask your child to find four living things. 3. For each, write one feature and the problem it solves.
flow.say: Every living thing near us is adapted too. A crow has a strong beak. What problem does that solve? Let's start with the problem.
flow.kid: Look out of the window for 10 minutes. Find four living things. For each one, write a problem and a feature.
flow.context: This is the first day of My Adaptation Notebook, a 3-day project. You find adaptations in living things around your own home.
flow.parent: Good examples: a crow's strong beak opens many kinds of food, so it can live on what people throw away. A pigeon puffs its feathers on cold mornings. Ants follow scent trails to food. A potted plant leans towards the window, towards the light.

flow.do: 1. In the kitchen or at the shop, find three more living things, or parts of them. 2. Look closely at one feature of each.
flow.say: A fish has gills and fins. A lotus stem is full of holes. What problems do they solve?
flow.kid: Find three more in the kitchen or the shop. A fish? A lotus stem? Write a problem and a feature for each.
flow.parent: If you buy a whole fish, look at its gills under the gill cover, and its streamlined shape. A cut lotus stem shows its air channels. A cabbage leaf shows its waxy coat with a drop of water.

flow.do: 1. Choose three more living things from this unit, from hot, cold, wet or dark places. 2. Make a page for each. 3. Share the whole notebook with someone at home.
flow.say: Now let's add three from far away. Can you explain each one, starting with its problem?
flow.kid: Add three more from this unit. Hot, cold, water or dark. Then show your notebook to someone.

check.q: Which is the best way to explain an adaptation?
options: Name the feature only: 'A camel has a hump.'
Say the problem, then how the feature helps: 'The desert has little water, so a camel's body loses very little.'
Say what it looks like: 'A camel is brown.'
check.why: An adaptation always solves a problem. Saying the problem first shows why the feature matters. Naming the feature alone does not say how it helps. The colour of an animal can be an adaptation too, but only if you say what problem it solves.

projects.context: This is a 3-day project. You make a notebook of ten living things and their adaptations, starting with ones you can see from your own home.

challenges.title: The Best Desert Leaf
challenges.problem: Design a paper leaf that keeps its water longer than a plain flat one. But a real leaf needs air and light to make food, so at least half of your leaf must stay open to the air.
constraints: Use one wet paper towel, the same size as a plain one.
At least half of the towel must be open to the air, not covered or rolled inside.
Test it beside a plain flat towel, under the fan, with the tissue touch test.
materials: 2 paper towels of the same size
a piece of milk-packet plastic or cling film
general: Fold the towel in half, so only half is open.
Cover half of it with plastic, like a waxy coat.
Roll it loosely, leaving half the outside showing.
creative: Make a pleated fan, like a folded paper fan, so the folds shade each other.
Give it a 'hairy coat' of shredded tissue that traps still air, like the hairy leaves of some desert plants.
Make holes only on the shady underside, as many real leaves do.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own desert leaf. Draw it, build it and test it. How much longer than the plain one did it stay wet?

flow.do: Read the problem and the rule about keeping half the leaf open.
flow.say: A leaf that is completely covered would keep its water, but it couldn't take in air to make food. So half must stay open. How can you still save water?
flow.kid: Your leaf must keep water. But half of it must stay open to the air. How?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Best Desert Leaf challenge. You design a paper leaf that saves water but can still take in air.

flow.do: Draw three ideas before building.
flow.say: Engineers draw before they build. Let's draw three different leaves.
flow.kid: Draw three ideas for your desert leaf.

flow.do: 1. Build your best idea with a wet towel. 2. Put it beside a plain flat wet towel under the fan. 3. Do the touch test every 15 minutes.
flow.say: Which stays wet longer, yours or the plain one?
flow.kid: Build your best idea. Put it beside a plain wet towel. Test them every 15 minutes.
flow.parent: Folding or pleating usually helps a lot, because folds hide part of the surface and shade each other.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here are some usual solutions, and some creative ones. Can you beat them?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ideas and the creative ones. Now invent your own.
flow.think: Rice leaves roll up only at midday and open again in the evening. Why is that better than staying rolled all the time?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You design a paper leaf that saves water, while keeping half of it open to the air.

challenges.title: Float Like a Water Hyacinth
challenges.problem: A water hyacinth floats because its leaf stalks are full of air. Build a floating raft, from home materials, that holds up 10 coins without sinking.
constraints: Use only drinking straws, aluminium foil, tape and a bottle cap.
It must float in a bucket for 2 minutes with 10 one-rupee coins on it.
No plastic bottles or boxes, which are too easy.
general: Tape straws side by side into a raft, with their ends sealed with tape so air stays inside.
Fold foil into a shallow boat with high sides.
Tape a bottle cap upside down under a foil sheet, to trap a pocket of air.
creative: Make swollen 'stalks' from foil wrapped loosely round air, like the spongy stalks of a water hyacinth.
Copy a lotus stem: bundle many sealed straws together, like its air channels.
Spread the coins out across the whole raft, so it does not tip.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own floating plant. Draw it, build it, and test it with 10 coins. How many more coins can it hold?

flow.do: Read the problem. Look at a picture of a water hyacinth, or a cut lotus stem.
flow.say: Water plants have air inside them, which helps them float near the light. How could we trap air in a raft?
flow.kid: Water plants float on air trapped inside them. How could you trap air in a raft?
flow.context: This is the first step of Float Like a Water Hyacinth. You build a raft that floats on trapped air, like a water plant.

flow.do: 1. Build a raft. 2. Float it in the bucket. 3. Add coins one at a time. 4. If it sinks, improve it and try again.
flow.say: Add the coins one at a time. Where does the water get in?
flow.kid: Build your raft. Float it. Add coins one by one. Does it sink? Make it better.
flow.parent: Straws only trap air if both ends are sealed. Pinch each end flat and wrap it with tape. Spread the coins out, or the raft tips and water pours in.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions, then invent one more.
flow.say: Here are some ideas. Which ones are most like a real water plant?
flow.kid: Look at the ideas. Which is most like a real water plant? Invent one more.

opts: A feature of body or behaviour that helps a living thing live in its habitat
quiz.why: An adaptation is a feature, like a camel's padded feet, or a way of behaving, like a lizard hiding at noon, that helps a living thing live and have young in its habitat.

quiz.p: Meena moves from Bengaluru to hot Chennai. After two weeks she starts to sweat sooner on hot days. What is this called?
opts: An adaptation passed on to her children
Acclimatising: her body getting used to a new place in her own life
quiz.why: Changes that happen in your own life, as your body gets used to a place, are called acclimatising. They are not passed on to your children. Picking 'an adaptation passed on' mixes up the two.

quiz.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3, wets three paper towels the same way. He leaves one flat, rolls one up tight, and covers one with plastic. Which one dries first?
opts: They all dry at the same time
quiz.why: Water escapes only where the towel touches the air. The flat towel has all of its surface open to the air, so its water escapes fastest. Rolling hides most of the surface, and the plastic covers it.

quiz.p: Why is a cactus fat and round, with no flat leaves?
opts: So that little of it touches the dry air, and it loses water slowly
So that it can grow fast
So that birds can sit on it
quiz.why: A fat, round stem holds a lot of water with little surface. Like the rolled towel, it loses water slowly. Big flat leaves would lose water fast in the desert.

quiz.p: What is inside a camel's hump?
quiz.why: The hump is mostly fat. A camel saves water by losing very little of it, for example by letting its body warm up during the day instead of sweating. Picking 'water' is a very common idea, but Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen showed it is wrong.

quiz.p: A fennec fox lives in the hot Sahara Desert. It has very big ears. How do big ears help it?
opts: They help it hear the rain
Heat leaves its blood through the thin skin of its ears, which cools it down
quiz.why: Blood flows close to the skin in the big, thin ears, and heat escapes from it into the air. That cools the fox. An Arctic fox, which lives in the cold, has small ears that lose little heat.

quiz.p: A snow leopard lives in the snowy mountains of Ladakh. Which of these helps it most to keep warm?
opts: Thick fur that traps still air
quiz.why: The still air trapped in thick fur slows down heat escaping from the snow leopard's warm body. Big thin ears would let heat escape. A waxy coat saves water in plants. Webbed feet help in water.

quiz.p: Kavin, a boy in Class 3, puts 6 ice cubes close together in a block, and 6 more spread apart. Which melt more slowly?
opts: Both melt at the same speed
quiz.why: In the block, many sides of each cube touch only other cold ice, so less heat from the warm air gets in. Penguins huddle for the same reason: less of each body faces the icy wind.

quiz.p: How does a duck keep its feathers from getting soaked?
opts: It stays out of the water
It spreads oil from a gland near its tail over its feathers
Its feathers are made of plastic
quiz.why: A duck rubs oil from its preen gland over its feathers with its beak. Water then runs off in drops instead of soaking in.

quiz.p: Some mangrove trees grow in salty mud on the coast. Why do they have roots that stick up out of the mud?
opts: Because the mud under water has very little air, and these roots take in air
quiz.why: Wet mud has very little air in it. Roots that poke up out of the mud can take in air, so the tree's roots get what they need.

quiz.p: A cat's eyes shine in a torch beam at night. Why?
opts: Cats' eyes make their own light
A shiny layer at the back of the eye reflects the light back
quiz.why: Many night animals have a shiny layer at the back of the eye. It reflects light back through the eye, which helps them see in dim light. It does not make light.

quiz.p: Some fish live in dark caves and have no eyes. How do they find their food?
opts: They use their lateral line, which feels the water move, and many taste buds
quiz.why: Cave fish feel the water moving with their lateral line, and find food by taste and touch. In total darkness, eyes cannot help them.

items.p: Which animal is best suited to the hot, dry Thar Desert?
items.why: A camel's body saves water and copes with heat, so it can live in a desert.

items.p: Which animal is best suited to icy Ladakh?
items.why: A snow leopard has thick fur, a long thick tail and small ears, which keep it warm in the snow.

items.p: A camel's hump is full of water.
items.why: False. The hump is mostly fat. A camel saves water by losing very little.

items.p: A wet towel that is rolled up dries more slowly than one spread flat.
items.why: True. Rolling hides most of its surface from the air, so its water escapes more slowly.

items.p: Bats are blind.
items.why: False. All bats can see. Many small bats also use echolocation to hunt in the dark.

items.p: A feature that helps a living thing live in its habitat is called an ____.
items.why: An adaptation can be part of the body or a way of behaving.

items.p: Animals that are awake at night and rest by day are called ____.
items.why: Owls, bats and the slender loris are nocturnal.

items.p: Water turning into an invisible gas and going into the air is called ____.
items.why: Wet towels dry because their water evaporates.

items.p: Match each animal or plant to its adaptation.
items.why: Each feature solves a problem of that living thing's habitat.
pairs: fat stem with a waxy coat
thick fur and a long tail
huge eyes for seeing at night

items.p: Sort these features. Do they help with heat or with cold?
items.why: Big ears, burrows and a waxy coat help with heat and dryness. Fur, blubber, small ears and huddling help keep warmth in.
items: hiding in a burrow at noon

items.p: Why does a cactus have spines instead of flat leaves?
opts: Flat leaves would lose too much water in the dry air
items.why: Flat leaves have a big surface, and water escapes through it. Spines lose very little water, and also protect the cactus from thirsty animals.

items.p: Why do emperor penguins huddle together?
opts: So that less of each body faces the icy wind, and they keep warm
items.why: In a huddle, much of each penguin is next to other warm penguins instead of the icy wind. So they lose less heat.

items.p: Which helps a fish swim fast?
items.why: A streamlined body lets water slide past easily, and fins push and steer.

items.p: Draw a duck's foot under water. Show the skin between its toes.
items.a: A foot with three front toes joined by skin, spread out like a paddle.
items.why: The skin between the toes pushes water like a paddle, so the duck moves forward.
items.art: An outline of a duck standing in water, with its foot left blank.

items.p: Kavya puts all her plants close together in the shade on a hot day. Why does this help them keep their water?
items.a: The pots shade each other and hide from the hot wind, so less water evaporates from their leaves and soil.
items.why: Crowding together means less of each plant faces the sun and hot air, like penguins huddling against the cold.

items.p: Put the steps of the three wet leaves experiment in order.
a: Wet three towels the same way
Shape them: flat, rolled and covered
Put them side by side under the fan
Do the touch test every 15 minutes
Unroll and uncover them, and compare
items.why: First make the towels equal, then change only one thing, then check them all at the same times.
items: Do the touch test every 15 minutes
Wet three towels the same way
Unroll and uncover them, and compare
Shape them: flat, rolled and covered
Put them side by side under the fan

items.p: In the three wet leaves test, why must all three towels go under the same fan?
opts: So that only the shape and covering change, and the test is fair
So the fan dries them faster
items.why: If one towel had more wind, we could not tell whether its shape or the wind made it dry faster. A fair test changes only one thing.

items.p: Ravi, a boy in Class 3, coats one spinach leaf with petroleum jelly and leaves another plain. After 4 hours the plain leaf is floppy. What does this show?
opts: A coat on the surface slows down the water escaping from a leaf
items.why: The jelly covered the leaf's surface and its tiny holes, so the coated leaf kept its water and stayed firm. Desert plants have a thick waxy coat that does the same.

items.p: A camel's body warms up by about 6 degrees on a hot day, and cools down at night. How does this help it?
opts: It saves the water it would use up sweating to stay cool
items.why: Sweating cools a body but uses up water. By letting itself warm up, the camel sweats much less, and the night air cools it down again for free.

items.p: An Arctic fox has small ears. A fennec fox in the desert has huge ears. Why the difference?
opts: Small ears lose less heat in the cold, and big ears get rid of heat in the desert
The desert fox needs to hear better
items.why: Heat escapes from the blood through the thin skin of the ears. In the cold, small ears keep warmth in. In the heat, big ears help the fox cool down.

items.p: Why do some mangrove trees push salt out through their leaves?
opts: Because they grow in salty sea water, and too much salt would harm them
To make the leaves taste good
items.why: Mangroves grow where the sea comes in every day. Some keep salt out at their roots, and others, like the grey mangrove, push the extra salt out through their leaves.

items.p: The slender loris of South India has huge eyes. Why?
opts: It is awake at night, and big eyes collect more light
items.why: The slender loris is nocturnal. Big eyes let in as much light as possible, so it can see insects in the dark.

items.p: A cave fish has no eyes, but it has many more taste buds than a river fish. How do the extra taste buds help it?
opts: They help it find food in the dark by taste
items.why: In total darkness, eyes cannot find food, but taste and touch can. Many cave fish have more taste buds and a bigger lateral line.

items.p: Changes your body makes in your own life, like sweating sooner after two weeks of hot weather, are passed on to your children.
items.why: False. That is acclimatising, and it is not passed on. Adaptations of the body are passed on from parents to young.

items.p: A lotus stem has holes inside it that carry air down to the parts under the mud.
items.why: True. You can see the holes when you cut a lotus stem, sold as kamal kakdi or thamarai thandu.

items.p: The row of sensors along a fish's side that feels the water move is called the ____ line.
items.why: The lateral line lets fish sense movement around them, even in the dark.

items.p: Finding things by making sounds and listening for echoes is called ____.
items.why: Small bats and dolphins use echolocation.

items.p: Sort these living things by the main problem their adaptation solves.
items.why: Each feature answers one problem: water, cold or darkness.

items.p: Choose one animal from this unit. Write its problem first, then its feature, then how the feature helps.
items.a: For example: Ladakh is freezing. The snow leopard has thick fur. The fur traps still air, which slows down heat escaping from its body.
items.why: A full answer has all three parts: problem, feature and how it helps.

items.p: Draw a fat cactus and a big thin leaf. Draw arrows to show where water escapes from each. Which has more arrows?
items.a: The thin leaf has arrows all over its big surface. The cactus has fewer arrows for its size.
items.why: Water escapes through the surface. The leaf has a lot of surface for the water it holds, the cactus has little.
items.art: An empty box with space for two drawings.

items.p: Six ice cubes are spread out on a plate. How many faces of each cube touch the warm air? Remember that one face sits on the plate.
items.why: A cube has 6 faces. One sits on the plate, so 5 touch the air.

items.p: Six ice cubes are pushed into a block of 2 rows of 3. How many cube faces touch the air now? Count the 6 tops and the faces around the edges.
items.why: There are 6 top faces. Around the edge, the long sides show 3 faces each and the short sides show 2 each: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 = 10. 6 + 10 = 16. Spread out, they showed 30. So the huddle showed only about half as many faces to the air.

items.p: A yak would struggle in the plains of Tamil Nadu in summer. Why?
opts: Its thick coat holds in so much heat that it would overheat
There is no grass in Tamil Nadu
items.why: An adaptation that helps in one place can be a problem in another. The coat that keeps a yak warm in Ladakh would make it dangerously hot in a Tamil Nadu summer.

items.p: A shark is a fish and a dolphin is a mammal. Why do they have such similar shapes?
opts: Both must swim fast in water, and that problem led to the same shape
items.why: Unrelated living things in similar places often end up with similar shapes. Scientists call this convergent evolution.

items.p: Lamarck said a giraffe's neck grew longer because giraffes stretched. August Weismann cut the tails off mice, generation after generation. What did the baby mice show?
opts: They were born with shorter tails
They were always born with full tails, so a change made to a parent's body was not passed on
They were born with no tails
items.why: Every baby mouse had a full tail. A change to the parents' bodies in their own lives was not passed on. That was one test against Lamarck's idea.

items.p: A wood frog freezes solid in winter and thaws in spring. What protects its cells from breaking?
opts: Sugar that floods its body before it freezes
items.why: Before it freezes, the frog's liver floods its body with sugar, which keeps the inside of its cells from freezing.

items.p: Which living thing's adaptation is a way of behaving, not a part of the body?
opts: A desert lizard hiding in its burrow at noon
items.why: Hiding at noon is something the lizard does. Spines and webbed feet are parts of the body.

items.p: Why might a cactus grow slowly?
opts: Opening its tiny leaf holes only at night lets in less air for making food
items.why: Saving water has a cost. With its stomata closed by day, a cactus takes in less air, and it needs air to make food.

items.p: A plant that is completely covered in plastic would save water, but could not take in the air it needs to make food.
items.why: True. Leaves need air coming in through their tiny holes to make food. A real leaf must balance saving water with letting air in.

items.p: A polar bear's hairs carry sunlight down to its skin like glass tubes.
items.why: False. In 1998, Daniel Koon tested this, and the hairs hardly carried light at all. The fur keeps the bear warm mostly by trapping still air.

items.p: Unrelated living things ending up with similar shapes because they live in similar places is called ____ evolution.
items.why: Cactuses and euphorbias, and sharks and dolphins, are examples.

items.p: Bergmann said animals of the same kind are bigger in colder places. Many animals do not follow this rule. Write one reason a scientist might give for why a big body could help in the cold, and one reason the rule might not always hold.
items.a: A big body has less outside for its size, so it loses heat more slowly. But food, enemies and other things also change how big an animal grows.
items.why: A good answer gives a reason for the rule and a reason it might fail. Scientists still argue about it.

items.p: Your rolled towel stayed wet inside. Explain, in your own words, what this tells you about why a cactus is fat and round.
items.a: Water escapes only from the outside, where the air touches it. A fat, round cactus has little outside for all the water inside it, so it keeps its water, like the inside of the roll.
items.why: A full answer links the towel's hidden inside to the cactus's small surface.

items.p: A bat hears its world, a cave fish feels its world through the water, and you see yours. Do you think they live in the same world? Give a reason.
items.a: Any thoughtful answer. For example: It is the same cave, but each animal meets it through a different sense, so each knows a different side of it.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A good answer gives a reason.

items.p: Design a plant for the Thar Desert. Label three features and the problem each one solves.
items.a: For example: a fat stem to store water, a waxy coat to stop water escaping, and very deep roots to reach water underground.
items.why: Each feature should answer a real problem of the desert: little water, hot sun or dry air.

applications: Builders in hot places use thick walls, light colours and shade, as desert animals do with burrows.
Gardeners group pots together and cover the soil with dry leaves, called mulch, to save water in summer.
Wetsuits for divers trap a thin layer of water and work as insulation, like an otter's fur or a seal's blubber.
Waterproof jackets and umbrellas are coated so water runs off in drops, like a duck's oily feathers.
Night-vision cameras, used by wildlife scientists and forest guards, collect very faint light, like a night animal's big eyes.
Ships and submarines use sonar, which works like echolocation, to find the sea floor and fish.
Road reflectors and the shiny strips on school bags reflect headlights back to the driver, like eyeshine.
Farmers choose crop varieties suited to dry or wet places, and scientists study rice that rolls its leaves in dry spells.
Doctors and scientists study the freezing wood frog to learn how to keep organs for transplant cold without damaging them.

open_questions.q: Exactly why did cave fish lose their eyes?
open_questions.why_open: Saving energy, side effects of better taste and touch, and broken genes that nobody weeds out may all play a part. Scientists still argue about how much each matters.

open_questions.q: How does a wood frog's heart know when to start beating again after it thaws?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know the frog's heart restarts as it thaws, but not fully how the signal begins.

open_questions.q: How well do adaptations keep up when a place changes fast, as the climate is changing now?
open_questions.why_open: Adaptations build up over many generations. Scientists are studying which animals and plants can change their behaviour or move in time, and which cannot.

open_questions.q: Does Bergmann's rule, that animals are bigger in colder places, really hold, and why?
open_questions.why_open: Many animals follow it and many do not. Scientists still argue about how often it holds and what causes it.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of cave animals live in India's caves?
open_questions.why_open: Many caves in Meghalaya and elsewhere have hardly been explored. New kinds of fish and other animals are still being found.

open_questions.q: How do penguins in a huddle decide when to move?
open_questions.why_open: Filmed huddles move in small waves, but how each bird decides to take a step is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the three wet leaves test, Lakshmi weighed her towels. In one hour, the flat towel lost 18 grams of water. The covered towel lost only 2 grams. How many times as much water did the flat towel lose?
maths.explain: The flat towel lost 18 grams and the covered towel lost 2 grams. 18 divided by 2 is 9. So the flat towel lost 9 times as much water. Check: 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 18.
maths.context: This is about the three wet leaves test. You wet three paper towels the same way, leave one flat, roll one and cover one, and see which keeps its water.

chart.title: Water lost in one hour (made-up example)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'it lost more' tells us little. Dividing tells us how many times more, so we can see how much a waxy coat helps.

maths.problem: In the huddle test, six ice cubes spread apart each had 5 faces touching the air. In a block of 2 rows of 3, the cubes had 16 faces touching the air altogether. How many faces touched the air when they were spread apart? How many fewer did the huddle have?
maths.answer: 30 faces spread apart, and 14 fewer in the huddle.
maths.explain: 6 cubes with 5 faces each is 6 groups of 5, which is 30. The huddle had 16. 30 take away 16 is 14. So the huddle hid 14 faces from the warm air, nearly half of them.
maths.context: This is about the huddle test. You put six ice cubes close together in a block and six spread apart, and watch which melt faster.
maths.why_maths: Counting the faces that touch the air explains the result. Fewer faces in the air means less heat can get in, so the huddle melts more slowly.

maths.problem: Bodil and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen measured a thirsty camel in the Sahara. Its body was 34 degrees Celsius in the early morning and 40 degrees by late afternoon. How many degrees did it warm up during the day?
maths.explain: 40 take away 34 is 6. So the camel's body warmed up by 6 degrees. Your body stays close to 37 degrees all day. If it warmed up by 6 degrees, you would have a dangerous fever.
maths.context: This is about how a camel saves water. Instead of sweating to stay cool, it lets its body warm up during the hot day, and cools down at night.
maths.why_maths: Working out the difference shows how big the camel's daily change is, compared with yours.

maths.problem: In the three wet leaves test, Farhan did the touch test every 15 minutes. The flat towel was dry at the 4th check. The rolled towel was still wet inside at the 8th check. How long did each take?
maths.answer: The flat towel was dry after 60 minutes. The rolled towel was still wet inside after 120 minutes, which is 2 hours.
maths.explain: 4 checks of 15 minutes is 15 + 15 + 15 + 15 = 60 minutes. 8 checks is twice as many, 120 minutes. So the rolled towel kept its water for at least twice as long.
maths.context: This is about the three wet leaves test. You check three wet paper towels every 15 minutes to see which dries first.
maths.why_maths: Counting in equal groups of 15 minutes turns the number of checks into a time, so you can compare how long each towel kept its water.

maths.problem: In the huddle test, the spread-out cubes made 120 millilitres of meltwater in 30 minutes, and the huddle made 60 millilitres. Arjun says, 'If I spread the cubes even further apart, they will make even more meltwater.' Is he right? What would you test to find out?
maths.answer: Probably not much more. Once the cubes are apart, all 5 of their faces already touch the air. Spreading them further would not open up any more faces. You could test it by putting 6 cubes a finger-width apart and 6 cubes a hand-width apart.
maths.explain: The huddle made half as much meltwater, 60 out of 120, because it hid faces from the air. Spread-out cubes already show every face except the bottom. So spreading them further should change little. A fair test would change only the distance between cubes.
maths.context: This is about the huddle test. You compare ice cubes in a tight block with ice cubes spread apart.
maths.why_maths: Using the numbers to reason about faces helps predict what a new test will show, before doing it.

roots.context: We have learned how living things are suited to heat, cold, water and darkness. Now we ask what this tells us about living things and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: Your three wet towels held the same water, yet they dried at very different speeds. Water escapes only through a surface that touches the air. Rolled up or covered, a towel kept its water for hours. So a cactus's shape and waxy skin save its water every minute, even while it rests.
deep_truth.habit: We think of saving water as something done on purpose, like turning off a tap. A cactus also decides things, such as when to open its tiny leaf holes. But much of its saving is done by its body's shape and coat, all the time.
deep_truth.evidence: The flat towel was dry within an hour or two. The rolled towel was still wet inside, and the covered towel was wet nearly all over. The same water, the same towel and the same fan: only the shape and covering changed.

three.who_am_i: Your body is adapted too. You sweat to cool down, and you curl up under a blanket to keep warm.
three.what_is_life: Every living thing carries features that suit the place its parents and grandparents lived, going back many generations.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth has burning sand, ice, deep water and dark caves, and living things live in all of them.

roots.thread: All living things on Earth share one family tree, going back to the first living cells. From that one beginning came the camel, the snow leopard, the cave fish and the cactus. Each place on Earth set its own problem: keep water, keep warm, move in water, find food in the dark. Life found a different shape for each. A dolphin's flipper, a bat's wing and your hand even have the same bones inside, shaped in different ways.

teachings.teaching: The stalk of a water flower grows as long as the water is deep. In the same way, a person rises as high as their spirit.
teachings.link: Thiruvalluvar used a real fact about water plants: a lily's stalk really does grow longer in deeper water, so the flower reaches the surface. A living thing's body follows the needs of its place.

teachings.teaching: Living plants are soft and full of sap. When they die, they become dry and brittle.
teachings.link: In the jelly coat test, the plain leaf lost its water and went limp. Keeping water inside is part of staying alive, and desert plants are shaped to do it.

science.text: All living things share a common ancestry. The same bones are found in a dolphin's flipper, a bat's wing and a human hand.
Unrelated living things in similar places often end up with similar shapes. Scientists call this convergent evolution.

other_view.view: No one planned a camel or a cactus. Over many generations, the ones that happened to have features suited to the place survived and had more young. The fit between a body and its place is the result of who survived, not of anyone's purpose.

practice.title: Curl up, stretch out
practice.say: Let's lie on the floor. First, curl up into a tight ball, knees to your chest, arms round them. Stay still and breathe slowly five times. Notice the warmth between your arms and your tummy. Now stretch out wide, like a starfish, arms and legs spread. Breathe five times. Notice the air touching more of your skin. Which felt warmer? Your body did that by changing shape, without making any new heat.
practice.kid: Lie down. Curl up into a tight ball. Breathe slowly five times. Feel the warmth. Now stretch out wide like a starfish. Breathe five times. Which felt warmer?

ask: A cactus saves water every minute just by its shape. Is a body's shape a kind of knowing how to live?
The camel's way of saving water took many generations to build up. Is a camel calf born already knowing the desert?
A cave fish meets its world by touch and taste, and you meet yours mostly by sight. Which of you knows the cave better?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, in a city flat, with the materials listed. The three wet leaves test uses paper kitchen towels, or equal pieces of old cotton cloth. The covering is a piece of milk-packet plastic with 5 pin holes, because petroleum jelly does not spread well on wet paper. Under a fan in dry weather, the flat towel dries in about an hour, and the rolled towel stays wet inside for 2 hours or more. In humid monsoon weather everything takes longer, so the step says to keep checking or use a sunny window. The tissue touch test lets a child see wet, damp or dry without a scale. The huddle test needs 12 cubes from one tray, and plates kept out of sun and fan. In a warm room the difference shows within 20 to 30 minutes, and pouring the meltwater into two glasses makes it easy to see. The jelly coat test uses market spinach, which wilts within a few hours under a fan. Thicker potted-plant leaves may need overnight. The model eyes need a properly dark room, and the torch held beside the eyes. The ripple, whisker and webbed hand activities need a grown-up close by, and the plastic bag goes only on the hand. Both games work in a flat. Huddle Up needs three or more people, and Survive the Place can be played alone. Timings were checked step by step. The spine fits about 85 minutes: intro, the three wet leaves test, explanations, roots and quiz.

how_we_found_out.story: For hundreds of years, many people believed that a camel carries water in its hump, or in special pockets in its stomach. How else could it cross a desert for days without drinking? In the winter of 1953, two scientists set out to test it. Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen, from Denmark, and her husband Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, from Norway, took their equipment to Béni Abbès, an oasis in the Sahara Desert in Algeria. They kept camels without water, weighed them, took their temperatures and measured everything they lost. They found that the hump is mostly fat, not water. The stomach held no store of water either. Instead, a camel saves water by losing very little. A thirsty camel let its body warm up by about 6 degrees during the hot day, instead of sweating to stay cool. At night it cooled down again. It also made very little urine. A camel could lose water equal to a quarter of its body weight and still recover once it drank. Bodil later became the first woman to lead the American Physiological Society, in 1975.
how_we_found_out.who: Bodil Schmidt-Nielsen and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen, scientists who studied how animals' bodies work
how_we_found_out.when: 1953 to 1954, at Béni Abbès in the Sahara. Their camel temperature results were published in 1957
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought a camel's hump, or pockets in its stomach, held a store of water. The Schmidt-Nielsens measured camels in the Sahara and found the hump is fat and the stomach holds no water store. Camels survive by losing very little water, partly by letting their bodies warm up by day.
